title: Second Intergenerational Climate Conversation at the Archeological Park of Ostia Antica brings young voices to the forefront of heritage adaptation
content:
The Second Intergenerational Climate Conversation, held from 27-28 October 2026 at the Archeological Park of Ostia Antica, Italy, a European Heritage Label site, brought together young people, heritage professionals, and environmental experts to explore climate adaptation measures for the heritage site.

With youth participation at its heart, the event allowed younger generations to share their perspectives, present their ideas and actively contribute to discussions on climate adaptation through workshops, presentations and site visits.

Organised within the framework of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub by ICLEI Europe, together with Project Leader Europa Nostra and partners Youth.Heritage.Europe. and the European Heritage Label Bureau, the conversation connected local experiences with wider European perspectives, highlighting the importance of empowering young people to take an active role in safeguarding cultural heritage and building climate resilience.

title: SIREH photography exhibition at COP17 in Yerevan links natural and cultural heritage
content:
From 19 to 30 October 2026, Yerevan hosted the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP 17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). It was the largest international gathering Armenia ever held, and it carried a particular weight: COP17 marked the first global review of collective progress on the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the moment when the world measures how far ambition has turned into action.

Alongside the negotiations, the Green Zone at the Karen Demirchyan Complex opened to the public, hosting hundreds of scientific, cultural and environmental initiatives, and drawing delegates, researchers, students and Yerevan residents into the same rooms.

title: Returning Hrvoje’s Missal: Cultural Rights and Shared Stewardship of Displaced European Heritage
content:
Cultural heritage is not only about preservation, ownership, or museum access. It is also a matter of cultural rights: the right of communities to encounter their foundational objects within the historical, linguistic, and spiritual context that makes them intelligible (CoE 2005). That is especially true when an object is not merely an artwork, but a liturgical, legal, and linguistic witness whose meaning depends on the tradition that produced it. In such cases,  restitution is not simply the relocation of property; it is the repair of a contextual mismatch.

The international dialogue on cultural heritage management has increasingly pivoted from a defensive, retentionist logic toward a more proactive language of restorative justice (Visconti 2023; Campfens 2023; Knudsen et al. 2022). Türkiye has become one of the most prominent and articulate voices in this evolving conversation. Its position is not limited to the recovery of objects removed from Anatolia; Türkiye has also increasingly participated in wider international debates concerning cultural sovereignty, historical displacement, and the legitimacy of imperial-era removals (CP 2025; TM 2025; Ditmars 2026; Geranpayeh 2026).

title: Where the Streets Have Female Names (And Sound Like Them)
content:
Rome is a lasagna of history: the remains of ancient homes form the bottom layer, covered by the medieval streets that rise above them; baroque churches decorate the stack; and modern traffic winds through the gaps like the top layer of the besciamella white sauce. The city looks like a thick slice of more than two millennia of urban planning, for the most part baked by men. 

But what if we experienced The Eternal City not only by what we see around us, but by how it makes us feel? And what if women, whose voices have not been included in the official recipe, became the cooks of its newest level?

According to the Mapping Diversity research by the European Data Journalism Network, of the 16,691 streets and squares in Rome, 8,067 are dedicated to named individuals. Of these, almost 93% honour men, and only about 7% honour women. The same research, conducted across 32 European cities, found the pattern repeated continent-wide: streets, statues, and squares overwhelmingly celebrate male political leaders, military figures, and cultural icons, while women remain largely absent from recognitions in the public space.

title: Artificial Heritage: Reimagining Cultural Heritage in an Era of Digital Transformation
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being used to recover historical documents and artifacts. Following the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, a library containing more than 1,800 papyri ended up carbonised in the ancient city of Herculaneum. Almost 2,000 years later, a 3D scanning technique adapted from medical imaging was used to virtually unwrap those scrolls (Vesuvius Challenge). A machine-learning method, capable of distinguishing ink from burnt papyrus, was then able to read the hidden text. This way, a corpus that once required a destructive opening became accessible through digital methods, creating a preservation surrogate and a new scholarly object. Since AI-enabled reading can produce distortions, temporary gaps, or even hallucinations, philologists and other investigators are still needed to interpret recovered fragments.

title: European Heritage Alliance and European Heritage Hub partners meet online to strengthen joint advocacy for cultural heritage in the next long-term EU budget
content:
On 27 October 2026, the European Heritage Alliance and  European Heritage Hub consortium met online to review recent EU policy developments and coordinate joint advocacy for cultural heritage in the next EU long-term budget.

Moderated by Sneška Quaedvlieg-Mihailović, Secretary General of Europa Nostra and Project Leader of the Hub, the meeting reaffirmed the relevance of the Alliance and Hub’s mission and the strength of the heritage sector as a cross-border movement, despite deep concerns over the cuts to the AgoraEU programme proposed by the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU.  

The meeting discussed several significant developments have taken place in the European cultural policy landscape that took place since the group’ last meeting in Brussels on 4 February 2026, Most notably, the Joint Declaration “Europe for Culture – Culture for Europe” was signed on 18 June 2026 by the Presidents of the European Commission, the European Parliament and the Republic of Cyprus on behalf of the rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union.

title: Join second ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ Forum in Mafra, Portugal, drawing a thread between music, heritage and climate change
content:
The ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ Forum is returning to Mafra. Taking place at the Royal Building of Mafra from 7-8 November 2026, the gathering will bring together leading European figures and experts from the fields of music, heritage, science, the environment and civil society, alongside youth representatives, around a shared ambition: to make music and listening catalysts for passing on heritage, fostering dialogue and strengthening European cohesion.

Organised by Hub partner Centre Européen de Musique, ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ is held in the frame of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub, in collaboration with Europa Nostra, the Municipality of Mafra, and partner Centro Nacional de Cultura, which oversees the Europa Nostra Heritage Hub in Lisbon. The event is placed under the High Patronage of the President of the French Republic. Visits to cultural sites will also take place, thanks to the Museus e Monumentos de Portugal and Museu Nacional da Musica.

title: First Intergenerational Climate Conversation at Sagres Promontory connects cultural and natural heritage with climate adaptation
content:
The first Intergenerational Climate Conversation, held on 5-6 October 2026 at the European Heritage Label site of Sagres Promontory, Portugal, brought together heritage professionals, researchers, locals and participants from different generations to explore how cultural and natural heritage can adapt to a changing climate.

Organised within the framework of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub by ICLEI Europe, together with Project Leader Europa Nostra and partners Youth.Heritage.Europe. and the European Heritage Label Bureau, the event explored the connections between climate, biodiversity, traditional knowledge and cultural memory, asking what must be protected today to ensure that heritage remains meaningful for future generations.

Sagres provided a fitting setting for the conversation, as a place deeply connected to Portugal’s maritime history and natural environment.

title: Youth.Heritage.Europe. brings youth voices to third Policy Debate on responsible tourism and heritage
content:
How can cultural tourism support heritage conservation without placing additional pressure on the places and communities it celebrates? This question guided Youth.Heritage.Europe.’s third Youth Policy Debate, organised within the frame of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub.

With welcoming remarks from Jasna Popović, Secretary of Youth.Heritage.Europe, and a panel moderated by Sophia Dibbs, Youth.Heritage.Europe.’s Programmes Officer, the event on 30 September 2026 brought together Chiara Ronchini, Theo Alexandridis, Daphne Gerodimou, and Andrea Bringas to discuss responsible tourism and the role of young people in shaping heritage practices.

The discussion explored the tensions between attracting visitors, protecting heritage, and maintaining the quality of life of local residents. Theo Alexandridis, one of the Hub’s NextGen Heritage Ambassadors, outlined environmental deterioration, physical damage, and social displacement associated with overtourism. Examples from Barcelona, Venice, Amsterdam, and Dubrovnik illustrated how destinations are responding through visitor management and restrictions on cruise tourism.

title: “What We Chose to Save” exhibition and Cultural Resilience Forum highlight Ukraine’s extraordinary cultural heritage rescue efforts
content:
On 2 October 2026, more than 150 Ukrainian and international heritage professionals, civil society representatives, military personnel and partners gathered in Kyiv for the Cultural Resilience Forum: From Emergency Response to a System of Protection.  A central highlight was the opening of the exhibition “What We Chose to Save: Stories from Cultural Rescue Missions in Ukraine,” which documents the people, decisions and efforts behind the protection of Ukraine’s cultural heritage amid Russia’s ongoing war.

Initiated by the Ukrainian Fulbright Circle, which operates the Europa Nostra Heritage Hub in Kyiv, the exhibition grew out of rescue missions carried out across Ukraine between 2022 and 2026. Developed in the frame of the the EU-funded European Heritage Hub and in collaboration with the Agency for Cultural Resilience (ACURE) and the Maidan Museum (Museum of the Revolution of Dignity), it brings together testimonies of those working to safeguard cultural heritage under extraordinary circumstances.
